guards.rule: When a room label is read from the plan, the room outline it anchors must be built into the model; a label with no matching room outline is a lost room, not a detail to skip.

A bedroom's anchor piece (the bed) must be placed inside the room outline; if the solver cannot fit the drawn bed, it must re-solve the sleeping group around the bed's drawn centre rather than dropping the bed.

A balcony's primary furniture group (seating) must be placed inside the room outline; if the solver cannot fit the drawn pieces, it must re-solve the terrace group around the drawn anchor rather than leaving the space empty.

A piece whose top exceeds the sloped ceiling or roof line over its position must be rejected at placement (or the room flagged as too low for that fixture); a bathtub is never placed where the headroom over it is under 2.0 m.
Exterior cameras must be placed at a position and target that frame the house facade or entrance without foreground obstructions (cars, walls, trees) blocking the view.
Interior cameras must be placed at a free point with headroom inside the room, aimed at the room's main fixtures or group, never at a bare wall or outside the room bounds.

Scene checks that fail on multiple pieces in a level indicate a systemic build issue (e.g., model parts not joined, pieces floating); rerunning the build stage with the correct join/rest logic should resolve them.
Soft seat models must have their parts joined within 1 cm; if the model's parts are separated, the build stage must re-join them or swap to a model with properly joined parts.

Armchair models must have their backs and arms resting against the seat within 5 mm; if the model's parts are separated, the build stage must re-rest them or swap to a model with properly resting parts.

Scene checks that fail on multiple pieces in a level indicate a systemic build issue (e.g., pieces not resting on the floor, overlapping); rerunning the build stage with the correct placement logic should resolve them.
A scene check that fails on a level is a build-stage defect: the level's geometry is rebuilt, not patched per piece.

Under a sloped ceiling the build must cap every interior element (rig, doors, furniture, decor) at the slope height (UL128); a ceiling that pokes through the roof is a build-stage cap failure, fixed by rebuilding the level, not by moving one piece.

A drawn armchair that ends up behind the back of its sofa and cannot be rotated or moved within the drawn lock is a seating-group placement failure: the furniture agent must re-solve the whole seating group (sofa, coffee table, armchairs) as one unit so every seat faces the group centre.
A TV unit that ends up behind the back of an armchair is a seating-group placement failure: the furniture agent must place the TV on the wall opposite the sofa axis, not beside a seat.
A wall-hung storage piece that crosses the room outline by a few centimetres (<= 0.03 m deep) is within tolerance: it is flush against the wall and the outline is the wall face, not a clearance line.
A coffee table that overlaps an armchair is a seating-group placement failure: the furniture agent must keep the table clear of every seat's footprint when solving the group.
A drawn seat whose front use zone is cut off from the door walkway is a seating-group placement failure: the furniture agent must keep a 0.60 m walkway to every seat's front when solving the group.
A sofa whose front use zone is cut off from the door walkway is a seating-group placement failure: the furniture agent must keep a 0.60 m walkway to the sofa front when solving the group.

A drawn armchair that ends up behind the back of its sofa and cannot be rotated within the drawn lock is a seating-group placement failure: the furniture agent must re-solve the whole seating group so every seat faces the group centre.
A stove or counter piece whose back is off its wall by more than 0.03 m is a fit error: snap it back onto the wall before any clearance check, so the 0.90 m aisle is measured from the true wall line.
A kitchen run must leave at least 0.90 m of clear aisle in front of it; if the drawn run is too deep for the room, shorten the run or shift it to the wall so the aisle meets the minimum.

A single armchair in a seating group must face the group's centre; if a rotation alone cannot do it without breaking clearance, the chair is re-seated (moved and turned) as one action, not rotated in place.
When an armchair's front use zone is blocked by a neighbour, the neighbour (or the chair) is re-seated so the zone is free; a move that only trades one clearance failure for another is not accepted.
A dining chair needs at least 0.81 m from the table edge to the wall or piece behind it; if the drawn chair is too close, the chair or the table is shifted so the pull-out space meets the minimum.
An armchair must not stand behind the back of a sofa facing it; it is turned to face the seating group's open side, and if that faces a wall it is re-seated to a free spot.

A double bed needs at least 0.60 m of free walkway on each side; if the room is tight, the bed is centred or shifted to the wall so both sides meet the minimum, and a retype that drops the bed is refused.

A wardrobe needs at least 0.80 m of clear space in front for the doors to open; if the room is tight, the wardrobe is shifted along its wall or a shallower model is used so the front clearance meets the minimum.

A drawn shower whose depth is below the real product minimum (0.70 m) but within 30 % of it is a misread size, not a valid product: the code must either correct the depth to the nearest real size or accept it as a walk-in tray, and must not flag it as 'outside product sizes' when the width is in range.
A bed that cannot clear 0.60 m on its free side in a 14 m2 bedroom must be swapped to a narrower model (<=1.45 m) rather than moved, since the room width is fixed by the walls.
A wardrobe whose front clearance is under 0.80 m in a bedroom should be swapped to a shallower model (<=0.57 m deep) to free the aisle, not moved, because the wall span is fixed.
When a sofa's front zone is blocked by another piece, the room's AI pieces must be re-solved as a group so the blocking piece moves, rather than swapping the sofa model.
A coffee table not in front of the sofa is a group-layout error; the seating group must be re-solved so the table sits in the sofa's front zone.
An armchair that is too far from and misaligned with the coffee table is a seating-group layout error; the group must be re-solved.
An armchair facing the back of another piece is an orientation error within a seating group; the group must be re-solved so all pieces face the group centre.

A flat 2D image of furniture standing on the floor is a rendering error caused by a piece that was not properly built in 3D; the room must be re-laid out so the piece is rebuilt with a proper 3D model.
A kitchen aisle under 0.90 m in front of the counter is a layout error; the kitchen run must be re-solved to free the aisle.
An armchair that does not face its seating group is an orientation error; the group must be re-solved so all pieces face the group centre.
A bed that cannot clear 0.60 m on its free side in a 16 m2 bedroom must be swapped to a narrower model (<=1.45 m) rather than moved, since the room width is fixed by the walls.
relayout_room

When a drawn piece is already typed and is drawn largely inside a larger piece of the same type in the same room, treat it as a duplicate of that piece (one item drawn twice) and drop the smaller one, instead of keeping it as a second piece that cannot be built.

When a drawn piece is already typed and is drawn largely inside a larger piece of a different type in the same room, treat it as a part of that piece (e.g. a seat cushion) and drop it, instead of keeping it as a separate piece that cannot be built.
A stair room whose stair fills the room and whose only camera point is inside the stair is shown by the adjacent hall's camera, not by its own interior camera.
Every drawn piece that is not built must be explained by a warning, a review entry or a symbol record; an untyped piece left unexplained is a loss.
none
An interior camera of a wet room must frame the room's primary fixtures (toilet, basin, shower/bathtub); a view that omits them is a bare-wall shot and is re-posed to show them.
A bedroom render must show the bed as the room's anchor; a camera that crops the bed out is re-posed to include it.
An interior camera of a wet room must frame the room's primary fixtures; a view that omits them is re-posed to show them.
A bedroom that is furnished with a desk and office chair in addition to a bed is a bedroom with a work corner, not a misread; the presence of the bed_double in the room's piece list is the anchor.
A hall render must show its main piece (shoe cabinet, console, stair); a camera that frames only a bare wall is re-posed to include the anchor.
An exterior or balcony render must show a finished outdoor environment (ground, planting, sky with depth); a flat grey placeholder is re-set with site items and a ground look.
An opening read from the documents must be cut through its wall; a door ray that still hits the wall means the cut was not applied and the build stage must re-run the opening cut.
A wall decor item must not overlap a wall fixture (basin, mirror, cabinet); the wall-item pass must raise, move or drop the item so it clears the fixture.
A wall decor item must not overlap a wall fixture; the wall-item pass must raise, move or drop the item so it clears the fixture.
A hung wall item must not hang over a window opening; the wall-item pass must move it to a free wall span or drop it.

A hung wall decor item must never occupy the same wall span and height band as a built wall fixture (basin, mirror, cabinet); the wall-item resolver must test decor against fixtures and re-place or drop it.
A hung wall decor item must never occupy the same wall span and height band as a built wall fixture; the wall-item resolver must test decor against fixtures and re-place or drop it.

A tall storage piece (tall_cabinet, wardrobe) must not be placed where the ceiling or roof slope drops below its height plus clearance; the fit stage must reject or relocate any piece whose top exceeds the local ceiling height, and the layout must keep tall storage off low-slope zones.

A habitable room's outer wall must not have a continuous blank stretch (no window or door) longer than a set limit; the layout stage must place at least one window or door on every long blank facade span of a living/sleeping room.
The exterior camera set must include a frontal view of the entrance (+y) facade at eye height, square to the facade, outside any building on the plot.
Where the terrain slope exceeds 1:3, the site stage must build a retaining edge (wall or stepped platform) along the steep boundary so the ground is stable and the building is supported.
Outdoor terrace/balcony furniture must use higher-detail, styled models that match the project's look, not generic low-detail placeholders.

An outdoor living space (terrace/balcony) must be styled as a designed space: include at least a rug or floor treatment, a light source, and a non-barren backdrop so it does not read as a bare grey box.
The main entrance door must be registered in site.entrances and its approach (steps/ramp/railing) must lead to a clearly defined, reachable door, not a dead-end wall.
A bathroom's wet fixtures (bathtub/shower) must use a complete, styled model that includes taps and fittings, not a bare module that leaves the fixture looking unfinished.
Every interior camera that must show a door from the documents must actually frame that door; the camera stage must verify the door is in the view and re-aim if not.
The exterior camera set must include a frontal view of the entrance (+y) facade at eye height, square to the facade, positioned outside any building on the plot.
A retaining wall or garden-bed edge must use a material that matches the building's facade style, not bare untextured concrete.
An interior bathroom camera must frame the washbasin (and its mirror) as the room's focal fixture, not a tub rim or a bare wall.
A bathroom camera must show the washbasin and mirror; a pose that only shows a bare tiled wall is not a valid bathroom view.
The site ground must carry a real lawn/ground texture, not a single untextured green plane, so outdoor spaces read as designed.
A balcony/terrace must be furnished as a lounge set (seating plus a table and plants), not left with only a couple of plants.
A kitchen counter's top must sit at working height (~0.90-0.97 m); a model whose top is ~1.18 m is the wrong model for the piece.
A camera must not crop a foreground piece in half; frame the complete piece and the view it looks out to.
A retaining/plot wall must carry a stone or cladding finish that matches the facade, not bare untextured concrete.
An interior bathroom camera must frame the washbasin (and its mirror) as the room's focal fixture, not a bare wall.
Every main facade, including the entrance (+y) facade, needs a frontal exterior view at eye height (1.5-1.7 m).
A sofa placed on an outdoor terrace must use an outdoor-rated model, not an upholstered indoor sofa.
A coffee table placed on an outdoor terrace must use an outdoor-rated model, not an indoor one.

A built piece must match its drawn footprint within 0.05 m; when the current model's size differs from the drawn size, swap to a library model whose dimensions match the drawing (never a model already refused as unusable).
A wall-hung toilet with a visible cistern plate that reads disjointed in a small bathroom should be swapped for a compact, cohesive model that fits the room's height and clearance.
Paired seating pieces in the same room must use the same model or a visually coherent set; a mismatched second piece is swapped to match its partner.
A generic, cheap-looking garden piece that reads as a placeholder in a stylish modern terrace is swapped for a model that matches the project's design language.
A drawn piece larger than 4.5 m on a side is a cluster of furniture, not a single piece; the reading stage must split it into individual pieces or type it as a group before the furniture stage.
An interior camera in a hall must show an open door leading to a furnished room, not a closed door and a bare wall; the camera is re-aimed to show the open door and the room beyond.
The facade material must match the family's facade scheme; if the scheme requires white render over a stone base, the facade slot is set to a white render look, not stone.
A sofa with no front set must have its front oriented towards the most open floor and its partner across the room; the code's suggested direction is used.
An interior camera in a bathroom must show an open door leading to a furnished room, not a closed door filling the frame; the camera is re-aimed to show the open door and the room beyond.
A bathroom's storage set must be complete; if a twin bathroom has a tall_cabinet and this one does not, the bathroom_set group is completed with the missing member.
An interior camera that renders entirely black/empty must be re-aimed to a free point with headroom that shows the room's main fixtures; the camera is moved to a valid pose.
A hall with multiple doors needs a console or coat storage to be usable; the entrance group is completed with the missing member.
A 'not built' note that names a piece already present in the room's built piece list is a stale record, not a loss: verify the piece is in the room before treating the note as a finding.
A hall is not required to contain a stair when the level has a dedicated stair room; do not flag a hall as under-furnished for lacking a stair that is correctly placed in its own stair room.
A double bed's sleeping set requires a nightstand on each side of the head; when one side is free, the missing nightstand must be placed there.
An interior camera must frame the room's main seating group (sofa, coffee table, armchair) so the room reads as a whole.
A bathroom set includes a tall_cabinet (storage) in addition to the shower, toilet and washbasin; a twin bathroom missing it is incomplete.
A bathroom camera must show the room's main fixtures (bathtub/shower, washbasin, toilet) so the room reads as a whole.
A bedroom camera must include the bed in its frame so the room has a visual anchor.
A terrace camera must include the seating furniture in its frame so the space reads as furnished.
A bedroom camera should show the room's main furniture and its door to the hall so the room's access is visible.
A bathroom camera must show the room's main fixtures (shower/bathtub, washbasin, toilet) so the room reads as a whole.
A balcony or terrace of 15 m2 or more is furnished as a seating set (a lounge group), never as a single chair.
An interior camera must frame at least one fixture or piece of value; a bare wall, corner or switch is not a view.

When the family's facade scheme calls for a stone base under a white render, the facade slot is set to the render and the stone is kept only on the plinth/base slot; the stone is never cladded over the whole facade.
The sheets stage must resolve every sheet question it writes before it ends; it may not end 'pending'.
A piece's front is read from the plan crop, not from the AI's default; when the AI front is on the short side of a long piece, the reading is an error and the stage must re-read it.
A built decor item that fails a scene check must be re-built or removed; the scene stage must not leave a failing item in the level.
The big loop must run enough cycles to raise the house score; stopping at 0 cycles with no score gain is a failure.
An opening must be cut through its wall; a door ray that hits the wall means the opening is not cut and must be fixed.
A drawn piece without a front (front_inferred) is given the direction its front faces, read from the plan crop; the side that looks into the most open floor, towards its partner, is the front.
A drawn piece without a front (front_inferred) is given the direction its front faces, read from the plan crop; the side away from its wall or towards its partner is the front.
A piece built below the library level is a fitting error: the fit must keep the piece at or above the library floor, and a parametric mesh that cannot be placed there is refused, not built.

Views marked for review by the render check must be resolved by fixing the underlying cause (camera position, door state, or layout) before the render is accepted; a view that cannot be fixed by a camera move is a layout or build issue, not a render issue.
Inside doors stand open by default (UL116): the build must record a leaf state for every inside door, and a door with no leaf state recorded is treated as open, not closed.
A door a view sees into a room worth showing stands open (UL126): the build must open the door so the view shows the room beyond, and a door with no leaf state recorded is treated as open.

When a bed's headboard is off the wall (F3) and the side clearance is under 0.60 m (G5), the bed must be moved to a wall span that gives both a flush headboard and >= 0.60 m side clearance; if no such span exists within 1.2 m of the drawn place, the room layout must be relayouted, not the bed moved piecemeal.
A living room's seating and dining sets must be drawn from one style family so the room reads as a designed whole, not a collection of random pieces.
Every bedroom's wall behind the bed must carry a feature finish (panelling or wainscot) to anchor the bed and add depth.
A living room's seating group must be anchored by a large area rug.
A hall must carry a console or a lit wall niche (H1, H4) so it is not a bare passage.
A living room's furniture must form a coherent group; a lone sofa, bench and plant is not a designed room.
A sectional sofa model must be a single welded body; its parts must not stand more than 1 cm apart.
A washbasin's lowest point must sit at floor level (within -0.005..+0.01 m); a model whose base is raised ~0.38 m is a wall-hung unit and must not be placed as a floor-standing basin.
A desk and its office chair must not cut each other; the chair's seat zone must clear the desk by at least the tolerance.
A model-fit check (M33) must not be reported against a piece whose type has no seat or back (e.g. potted_plant, side_table); the check should be skipped for non-seating types.
When a seating model's back or arm is detached from its seat by more than 5 mm (M33), swap to a library model of the same type whose geometry is integral.
A wardrobe model with a large glass pane in its door is not a standard wardrobe; swap to a solid-door wardrobe model of the same type and size.
An interior corridor camera must show the doors or the main circulation path, not a close-up of a wall detail.
A bathroom camera must show the main fixtures (shower, toilet, washbasin) with enough headroom to see the full height of the shower and mirror.
A shower screen must be transparent glass or a textured panel, not a flat opaque slab; swap to a library shower model with a proper glass screen.
A corridor camera must show the doors and circulation path, not a blank corner or featureless wall.
A kitchen render must include small appliances and decor on the worktop to look lived-in, matching the reference.
A wall_cabinet model that renders as a missing or invisible layer must be swapped to a library model that renders correctly.
A kitchen worktop must include small appliances or decor to look functional and lived-in.
A kitchen camera must show the main functional elements (fridge, stove, counter) without cutting them off.
When an armchair's design language clashes with the room's other furniture, swap to a model that matches the room's style.
When a dining table's design language clashes with the room's other furniture, swap to a model that matches the room's style.
A living room with a minimalist style should have a feature wall (fluted or slatted wood panelling) behind the main seating group to anchor it.
A full-height window in a living room must be dressed with layered curtains (a sheer behind a heavier drape) in the render, not left as bare glass.
A coffee table in a living room must be styled (books, a vase, small decor) in the render, never left as a bare surface.
A living room must be lit with layered warm light (downlights plus a warm lamp glow), not a single cold linear pendant and daylight.
A bathroom render must include wall art (a framed piece) so the walls are not bare.
An interior bathroom camera must be pulled back and raised to show the whole room (vanity, shower, toilet), not a low close-up of one fixture.
A window must be dressed with layered curtains (sheer plus drape), not left as bare glass.
A bed must be styled with layered bedding (duvet, throw, a blanket across the foot, euro shams and decorative cushions), not a single duvet and a few pillows.
An interior hall camera must show the hall, its floor and its main group, not be pressed against a wall on a single picture frame.
An office chair in a bedroom must be a calm, warm, light-wood piece that matches the bedroom palette, not a black leather corporate chair.
The wall behind a bed head must be a feature wall (fluted/slatted wood panelling or wainscot), not flat concrete.
A bed must be styled with layered bedding (duvet, euro shams, decorative cushions), not a flat sheet and a single runner.
A bathroom door must be a modern, neutral-toned door that matches the room, not a warm prominent wood door with a large handle.
An interior hall camera must show the room as a whole from a hero angle, not a corner and the side of a single wardrobe.
Armchairs in a living room must share one design era and a palette that harmonises with the sofas, not clashing teal and red pieces.
A coffee table must be a 3D model, never a flat 2D image standing on the floor.
A dining chair and its table must be from the same style family as the rest of the room, not a cheaper white spindle set.
A balcony or terrace program must include at least one potted plant and one soft or lighting element; a bare slab with only seating is not a finished outdoor space.
Upper-floor windows in living and bedroom rooms must carry curtains or blinds in the render; bare glazing reads as unfinished.
An exterior camera must be a clear eye-level (1.5-1.7 m) or a high view above the ridge; it must not be obstructed by a car or interior.
An interior room camera must frame the room's main group (basin, shower, toilet for a bathroom), not a detail crop of a corner.
A model whose back or arm stands more than 5 mm from its seat is a broken model; swap it for a model with a coherent frame.
An interior room camera must frame the room's main group, not a corner with a blank wall.
An interior room camera must frame the room's layout and main pieces, not a wall section and a small cabinet.
A living room with a dining area should have a feature wall (slatted wood or paneling) behind the main seating or dining zone to add depth.
An interior room camera must frame the room's main group (bathtub, toilet, washbasin for a bathroom), not a door frame and vanity.
An interior room camera must frame the room's main group, not a corner with a wall and the edge of the bathtub.
A bedroom should not be furnished with a corporate office chair; a residential chair or a reading chair fits the warm, residential style.
An interior room camera must frame the room's layout and main pieces, not a wardrobe filling half the frame.
Seating pieces in a living room must form a coherent group in style and color; a brown leather armchair clashes with a white boxy sofa and a black lounge chair.
The outdoor environment must have a path, a fence or hedge, and trees to make the render look like a designed landscape, not a grey-box visualization.
A terrace floor must have a material or finish (e.g., paving stone, wood decking) to read as a designed outdoor floor, not a bare grey slab.
The outdoor environment must have a path, a fence or hedge, and trees to make the render look like a designed landscape, not a flat, untextured green plane.

A balcony camera must frame the furnished terrace as a coherent space: the pose must show the seating group and the open edge (guard) together, and must not be a corner or bare-floor shot; when no pose of the room's own pieces passes, the camera is dropped rather than left on a bare corner.
A flush ceiling light must keep at least 2.5 m from a pendant light in the same room; when a pendant is present, the flush light is removed rather than left 2.34 m away.
A dining set must mix a bench with upholstered or wood chairs, not repeat a single molded plastic chair around the table.
A shoe_cabinet model must be a believable, finished cabinet (not a low-poly metal frame placeholder) and must match the house's style family.
An accent armchair must belong to the room's neutral palette; a second loud accent (orange) that clashes with the existing teal chair is a mismatched set.
A side table model must be a believable table (not a toy-like disc with random pegs) and must match the room's style.
A bedroom camera must show the bed and its nightstands (the room's anchor); a view that omits the bed is not a bedroom view.
The view outside a window must show the designed landscaping (planters, seating, trees) from the site plan, not a flat untextured green field with a simple fence.
Door frames and leaves must match the house's light, airy wood-slat aesthetic; dark heavy frames clash with it.
A terrace floor must be a finished, styled surface (decking, outdoor rug, or textured paving), not a bare concrete slab with a drain.
A bathroom camera must not be pressed against the door leaf; it must show the vanity and the room from a free point with headroom.
A bedroom camera must show the bed and its nightstand (the room's anchor); a view that omits the bed is not a bedroom view.
A bedroom camera must not be positioned too close to the door frame; it must show the bed and the room from a free point with headroom.
A kitchen camera must show the kitchen run (counter, stove, upper storage) and the room from a free point; a view that cuts off the main appliances is not a kitchen view.
A bedroom camera must not be buried at the foot of the bed; it must show the bed, the feature wall, and the room from a free point with headroom.

An interior camera must frame the room's anchor piece (the bed in a bedroom) and the main seating or work zone; a view that crops the anchor out of frame or tilts the horizon is a failed view and must be re-posed to show the anchor.

A furniture model whose style family (industrial/open-frame) clashes with the room's established style (warm classic wood) is a mismatched set and must be swapped for a model in the same style family.
An outdoor space (terrace, balcony) that is a flat untextured slab with no planters, seating or rug is an unfinished exterior and must be furnished with a terrace or balcony group.

A living room that is a clean but empty shell with mismatched furniture and no styling layers (art, styled surfaces, warm light) fails the client-ready standard and must be restyled by the furniture agent.
A room with bare walls and generic shelf contents (only a few books) lacks the curated styling layer (art, mirror, vase, leaning print) and must be restyled.
A door frame whose style (thick black industrial) contradicts the room's established style (light beige minimalist) is a style clash and must be re-materialled to match.
A bathroom camera that is too low and too close, framing only one fixture and cropping out the rest of the room, is a failed view and must be re-posed to show the full layout.
A bedroom camera that crops out the bed and frames only a wardrobe and door is a failed view; it must be re-posed to show the bed as the anchor.
A bedroom where the headboard sits on a flat untextured wall lacks the feature wall layer (fluted or slatted wood panel) that the reference sets; the agent must add it.
A window with only a single sheer panel lacks the layered curtain treatment (sheer behind a heavier drape on a ceiling track) that the reference sets; the agent must add the full treatment.
A living room that is a flat beige grey-box with mismatched sofa styles, bare walls and no feature wall, rug or art fails the client-ready standard and must be restyled by the furniture agent.
A living room that is a flat unstyled grey-box lacking feature wall, rug, wall art and cohesive lighting fails the client-ready standard and must be restyled.
A living room that is a flat grey-box attic with a single pendant, no rug, no wall art, no styled surfaces, and a sofa with cushions on the floor fails the client-ready standard and must be restyled.
A room where the sideboard, coffee table and dining table are completely bare with no books, vase, mirror or art print looks empty and unfinished; the agent must add styled surfaces.
A balcony that is a bare slab with no plants, rug, lighting or decor is an unfinished outdoor room and must be furnished with a balcony group.
A camera pressed against a foreground piece that blocks the view of the space is a failed view; it must be re-posed to show the room without the foreground piece filling the frame.
A balcony or terrace side table must be a clean modern or minimal model; a wicker or rustic model with random props is a taste failure in a modern house.
A balcony or terrace seating set must be coherent: matching armchairs, matching cushions and a side table in one style family.
An outdoor terrace must be rendered with defined floor and parapet materials and a coherent furniture set, not a grey-box slab.
An exterior presentation render must show real facade materials, landscaping and atmospheric lighting, not a grey-box massing void.
An exterior presentation render must show real facade materials, site design and lighting, and no unexplained openings.
A garage must be rendered with a door, floor and structure; an open pit in the ground is not a functional garage.

A drawn furniture piece that no rule or model can type must be resolved by the reading stage (typed, or marked not furniture with evidence) before the run ends; it must not be left 'unknown' and unbuilt.
Decor that cannot rest on its host without penetration must be re-seated or dropped, not left unbuilt.
Decor that cannot rest on its host (no top found) must be re-seated or dropped, not left unbuilt.
A cushion that cannot rest on its host (top too high over the back, insufficient footprint over the support) must be re-seated or dropped, not left unbuilt.

A decor item that cannot find a resting top on its built host after the second attempt is dropped from the build and reported as not rested, instead of being placed on the floor or on the nearest valid surface.
A decor item whose placement penetrates its host by more than 0.01 m is dropped from the build and reported, instead of being nudged to a non-penetrating position.
A cushioned seat model whose cushions are rendered sunken into the frame is a model-quality issue; the scene stage should flag such models for replacement rather than building them as-is.
The reading stage should read entities on off or frozen layers when the ledger shows they hold geometry the model needs, or explicitly record why they are excluded.
guards.target: # entities on layers that are off or frozen (or invisible) were not read

guards.rule: The reading stage should read or explicitly skip entity types like OLE2FRAME and WIPEOUT, recording the reason for the skip.
A camera dropped by the camera stage must carry a reason; a drop with no reason is a loss that must be restored or explained.
A window that is not visible in a view that must show it is a render framing issue; the render stage should adjust the view or flag the window as occluded.
A drawn block that no model element uses must be either mapped to a model element or recorded as a non-structural annotation with a reason.
Anonymous A$C-prefixed blocks under 0.3 m on a side are annotation/dimension fragments, not furniture: the reading stage must not list them as lost furniture.

A drawn block whose name is not a known furniture symbol and whose size matches a standard piece (e.g. ~0.8 x 0.8 m) must be typed by the reading stage from its size and room before it is dropped; untyped blocks of furniture size are a reading loss, not a detail.

A drawn block whose name is not a known furniture symbol and whose size matches a standard piece (e.g. ~1.6 x 2.9 m, a bed or sofa) must be typed by the reading stage from its size and room before it is dropped; untyped blocks of furniture size are a reading loss, not a detail.

A drawn block whose name is not a known furniture symbol and whose size matches a standard piece (e.g. ~0.6 x 0.6 m, a chair or table) must be typed by the reading stage from its size and room before it is dropped; untyped blocks of furniture size are a reading loss, not a detail.
A block recorded as site decor (sd_*) is intentionally not built into the house model; the ledger must not flag it as lost furniture.
A drawn block named for a building element (e.g. 'merdiven' = stair) must be typed as that element by the reading stage; a stair-sized block left untyped is a reading loss.

A drawn block whose name is a placeholder or annotation string (not a furniture/fixture symbol) and whose size does not match any room program is not a lost element; the reading may drop it without building it.
Auto-generated block names (prefix 'A$C') are annotation or leader artifacts, not furniture; the reading may drop them without building them.
A drawn block whose name is not a recognized furniture or fixture symbol and whose footprint does not correspond to a missing required piece in its room is not a lost element.
Entities on layers that are off or frozen in the source DWG are intentionally hidden by the author; the reading correctly skips them and they are not lost elements.
OLE2FRAME and WIPEOUT entities are not furniture or fixtures; the reading correctly does not build them.
Reading diagnostics about wall layer selection, column counts, and stroke pairing are informational warnings, not lost elements.
A symbol that both reading passes classify as not_furniture and keep as an obstacle is a correct reading decision, not a lost element.
A drawn element on a structural layer (e.g. 'A-BA') classified as a column is structure, not furniture; the reading correctly does not build it as a furniture piece.
A fixture under a sloped ceiling is capped at the slope height at its footprint; the cap is independent of the drawn size check, so a size refusal must not block the height fix.

When one room outline carries the labels of two or more rooms, the reading must split it at the missing wall before room assignment; a label with no matching room outline is a lost-room signal, not a duplicate.
A balcony or terrace with drawn furniture must have that furniture built and visible; an empty outdoor room is a fit failure, not a camera failure.
A stair opening in a hall or landing that drops to a lower level must be built with a guardrail or barrier along its open edge; the guard is part of the stair's set, not an optional detail.
A fixture under a sloped ceiling must be a model whose height fits the headroom at its position; the shower's height is checked against the roof, not just its drawn footprint.
An interior camera must be posed at a free point with headroom that shows the room's main group; a black frame means the pose is inside geometry and must be re-picked.
A soft seat's facing bodies must be joined so no part stands more than 1 cm apart; the build stage's join step is responsible for this.
A soft seat's back, back cushion and arms must rest against its seat with no gap over 5 mm; the build stage's rest plan is responsible for this.
Scene geometry checks (S1) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
Scene geometry checks (S2) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
Scene geometry checks (S4) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
Scene geometry checks (S6) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
A scene check that fails on a level must be re-run after the level's pieces are corrected; the build stage owns the scene assembly.
When an armchair's orientation is refused because rotating it breaks its group facing, the whole seating group must be re-solved so the armchair faces the group and the coffee table.
A tv_unit that stands behind the back of a seat and cannot be rotated without leaving the room outline must be re-placed by the room solver so its back is on a wall and it faces the seating.
A wardrobe that pokes through the room outline by a few centimetres should be swapped for a model whose depth fits the wall bay.
When a coffee table overlaps an armchair and every single move is refused, the seating group must be re-solved as a unit so the table clears the chairs.
An armchair whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the door must be re-placed by the room solver so the walkway is clear.
A sofa_corner whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the door must be re-placed by the room solver so the walkway is clear.
When an armchair's orientation is refused because rotating it breaks its group facing or faces a wall, the whole seating group must be re-solved.
A tv_unit that stands behind the back of a seat and cannot be rotated (back off wall) or swapped (fit rules) must be re-placed by the room solver against a wall facing the seating.
When a coffee table overlaps an armchair and every single move is refused, the seating group must be re-solved as a unit.
A stove whose back is a few centimetres off the wall is a misread centre; the code should snap it to the nearest valid wall spot.
A kitchen aisle narrower than 0.90 m in front of the counter must be re-solved by the room solver so the run is placed to give the required aisle.

A wardrobe (or any storage with a door or drawer front) placed against a wall must keep at least 0.80 m of clear floor in front of its opening face; the solver must reject any wall span shorter than the piece plus that clearance and, when no span fits, flag the room for a smaller or different storage piece rather than placing it with a blocked front.
A seating group's front clearance must be kept free of other pieces; the solver must not place a piece inside the front use zone of a sofa or armchair.
A nightstand must not stand in front of a window sill; it belongs at the head of the bed on the free side.
A dining table must not stand in front of a window sill; it belongs away from the glazing.
A chair must not stand in front of a window sill; it belongs at the table, away from the glazing.
An armchair must face the seating group, not stand behind the back of another piece.
A tv_unit must have its back on a wall; it must not float in the middle of the room.
A sofa's long side is its front; it must not be turned 90° against its product size.
An armchair's front clearance must be kept free of other pieces.
A piece placed by the decor stage must survive the agent stage; if the agent drops it, it must be re-added.
The agent stage must not drop a placed decor piece without recording it; a piece present after the decor stage and absent after the agent stage is a loss to be restored, not silently removed.

A stove that is a member of a kitchen run (module:kitchen_counter:kitchen_run) must be built as part of that run's model, not as a standalone object; the build stage must emit the run's full model (counter, sink, stove) so every planned member has a scene object.

A sink_kitchen that is a member of a kitchen run (module:kitchen_counter:kitchen_run) must be built as part of that run's model, not as a standalone object; the build stage must emit the run's full model (counter, sink, stove) so every planned member has a scene object.

When two drawn pieces of the same type overlap by more than 30% and one is clearly inside the other, the smaller is a duplicate drawing of the same object, not a second piece; the larger is kept and the smaller is dropped as a detail.

When two drawn pieces of the same type overlap by more than 15% and one is clearly inside the other, the smaller is a duplicate drawing of the same object, not a second piece; the larger is kept and the smaller is dropped as a detail.
A small piece drawn 80% or more inside a larger seating piece (armchair, sofa) is its seat cushion or built-in element, not a separate piece; it is dropped as a detail of the larger piece.

A room whose program is a stair core (stair fills the room, no free floor point) is not given an interior camera; it is shown by the adjacent hall's view instead, and the camera stage must skip it rather than report it as a lost view.

A drawn block in a kitchen whose size matches a small appliance (roughly 0.2-0.6 m) that the furniture vocabulary does not type must be recorded with an explicit 'appliance, not modelled' note (or a dedicated appliance type) so it is neither silently dropped nor left unexplained.

A layer whose name is a stair section or elevation view (A-MERDIVEN, A-merdiven görünüş) is a detail view, not plan furniture: the reading classifies it as a detail view and feeds it to the stair reader, and the ledger does not flag it as lost when the stair it documents is built.

A layer whose name is a decorative or sanitary fixture detail view (Deko_Vitrifiye, Piu_Vitrifiye) is a detail view, not plan furniture: the reading classifies it as a detail view and the ledger does not flag it as lost.
A stove drawn with a small gap behind it (its back parallel to the wall) belongs on the wall: the reading snaps its back onto the wall instead of leaving a visible gap.
A shower drawn with a small gap behind it (its back parallel to the wall) belongs on the wall: the reading snaps its back onto the wall instead of leaving a visible gap.
A toilet whose centre is closer than 0.38 m to a side wall or fixture is misread: the reading moves it to the nearest valid spot that gives the required side clearance.
A shower with less than 0.53 m clear in front is misread: the reading moves it to the nearest valid spot that gives the required front clearance.

A toilet is placed so its centre is at least 0.38 m from any side wall or fixture; if the drawn position cannot meet this, the fixture is moved to the nearest valid spot rather than swapped for a model that still fails the clearance.
A bathtub must have at least 0.53 m clear in front; if the drawn position cannot meet this, the fixture is moved to the nearest valid spot.
A shower must have at least 0.53 m clear in front; if the drawn position cannot meet this, the fixture is moved to the nearest valid spot.
An interior camera of a bathroom must show the room's main fixtures (washbasin, toilet, shower/bathtub) so the render reads as a functional bathroom.
A bedroom must show its bed as the anchor; if the bed cannot be placed with the required clearances (0.60 m along the sides, headboard on a wall), the room is re-laid out so the bed fits.
An interior camera of a bathroom must show the room's main fixtures (toilet, shower) so the render reads as a functional bathroom.
An interior camera of a balcony/terrace must show the room's main furniture (seating, side table) so the render reads as a designed outdoor living space.
An interior camera of a bathroom must show the room's main fixtures (toilet, washbasin, shower) so the render reads as a functional bathroom.
An interior camera of a bedroom must show the bed as the anchor so the render reads as a bedroom.
An interior camera of a bathroom must show the room's main fixtures (toilet, bathtub, washbasin) so the render reads as a functional bathroom.
An interior camera of a wet room must frame its fixtures (basin, toilet, shower/bath); a view that omits the basin makes the room read as unfinished.
A kitchen's run must be completed with its missing members (fridge, sink, stove, counter); a run without a fridge is not a kitchen.
A bedroom must be furnished as a bedroom (bed, nightstands, wardrobe); a desk-and-chair layout without a visible bed is a misread of the room's program.
An exterior render must show a real ground plane and site context (trees, hedge, court); a flat grey gradient reads as a placeholder.
Every opening must be cut through its wall; an opening whose ray hits the wall is not built.
A wall-mounted decor item must not overlap a wall fixture (basin, mirror, cabinet) on the same wall; the wall-item pass must raise it, move it along the wall, or drop it.
A wall-mounted decor item must not hang over a window opening; the wall-item pass must move it to a free wall span or drop it.

A hung decor item must never be placed on the wall span occupied by a washbasin or its mirror; the resolve pass must skip that span and use the next free wall, or omit the item if no free span exists.
Any outer wall span of a habitable room longer than 3 m must contain at least one window or door; the layout stage must add an opening if the drawing does not provide one.
Every project must include at least one frontal exterior camera view of the main entrance facade.
If the terrain slope is steeper than 1:3, the build stage must include a retaining edge or stepped foundation to support the structure.
Outdoor terrace furniture must use models rated for outdoor use (weather-resistant materials).
Indoor lighting fixtures (floor lamps) must not be placed on outdoor terraces; use outdoor-rated lighting instead.
Indoor storage furniture (bookshelves) must not be placed on outdoor terraces.
The inspector must read the room id of the target piece from the facts before judging its placement; a piece in an indoor living room is not on the terrace.

Every exterior door must be rendered with a modelled leaf and frame that match the window frames' material, and the space beyond an exterior door must be lit and textured (not a dark void) in the render.
Every door leaf and frame must be assigned a material that matches the project's window frame material (e.g. light wood) so that doors do not read as placeholder slabs.

A bathroom shower or bathtub model must include visible taps, a drain, and at least one accessory (towel rail or shelf) in its render; if the library model lacks these, the building stage must add them as separate fixtures or choose a model that includes them.
Every washbasin in a bathroom must be rendered with a mirror above it; if the library model does not include a mirror, the building stage must place a mirror as a separate fixture above the basin.
Every interior camera view of a room must show at least one door or window of that room, so the viewer can orient themselves.

Every exterior camera view must be positioned outside the building envelope, at a distance of at least 1.5 m from the nearest facade, at eye height (1.6 m) or an aerial height, and must not be under the roof overhang.
Every exterior wall, including retaining walls, must be assigned a material that matches the building's facade material so that no bare concrete slabs are visible.
Every bathroom must have a complete bathroom_set including a mirror above the washbasin and a towel rail; if the set is incomplete, the building stage must add the missing members.
The inspector must verify that the bathroom_set members are actually missing before flagging a missing_member finding; if the set is complete, the finding is a false alarm.
Every interior camera view of a bathroom must show the main fixtures (washbasin, toilet, shower/bathtub) so the room reads as designed.

Every bathroom must have a mirror above the washbasin and at least one styled surface (accent wall, shelf, or accessory); if the library models do not include these, the building stage must add them as separate fixtures.

Every outdoor scene must include textured ground (grass, paving, or gravel), at least 3 trees or shrubs with visible foliage, and a horizon that is not a hard line; the render stage must use high-quality ground and vegetation assets.

Every outdoor furniture piece must use a model that matches the project's style (e.g. scandinavian, modern) and has visible texture or design detail; plain generic models are not acceptable for outdoor scenes.
Every terrace or balcony must have a complete terrace_lounge group (at least 2 seating pieces, 1 table, and 2 plants) so it reads as a designed outdoor space.

A kitchen counter (kitchen_counter) is built at its standard working height (top at 0.90-0.95 m) regardless of the drawn footprint's height; a drawn counter taller than its working height is a misread of a tall unit or a wall cabinet, not a counter, and must be retyped or resized, never built as a counter at the drawn height.

A site area labelled as a pool (havuz) in the documents must be built as a pool outline in the model; if the site holds multiple pools, each documented pool area is built with its own outline and water surface, not left as an unbuilt label.
A site area labelled as a sunning terrace (guneslenme alani) in the documents must be built as a paved terrace outline in the model, not left as an unbuilt label.

A site area labelled as a parking area (otopark) in the documents must be built as a paved parking outline in the model, and at least one car model must be placed on it to show it is a parking area, not left as an unbuilt label with no cars.
Every interior door leaf is rendered open against its swing side by default; only entrance and terrace doors are closed.
A bathroom render must frame the vanity, mirror, shower and towel storage, not a bare wall above the tub.
A hall render must show the furnished room beyond, not be dominated by closed door slabs.
A living room must carry its full seating group (sculptural armchairs, round coffee table, lit TV console), not a plain sofa set.
A paved strip at the foot of a long glazed facade must run the full length of the facade, not stop short at one end.
The facade scheme is white render over a stone base, not stone from base to eaves.
In front of a glazed ground-floor facade the site must be a flat pale paved strip, not a raised walled terrace box.
A paved drive or stair path must lead on to the plot edge or a street, not end at the lawn.
An entrance canopy must carry a fascia, soffit and tie rods or brackets, not be a bare slab stuck out of the wall.
A house on a plot must show fenced neighbouring plots and a road coming to it; the drive must lead somewhere.
A drawn piece over 4.5 m on a side is a group of pieces, not a single furniture item; it must be split into its members and typed individually, not left untyped.
A door under a sloped ceiling needs at least 1.60 m of headroom; where the roof slope leaves less, a dormer or raised roof must be added at that spot.

A door under a sloped ceiling whose headroom is under 1.60 m at its wall and within 0.5 m along it must be flagged for a dormer or raised roof; the building stage must not lower the door to the roof line and leave it unusable.

When a bedroom's drawn bed leaves less than the nightstand depth (0.60 m) on one side, the sleeping set is complete with a single nightstand on the free side; do not flag the missing second nightstand as a defect.
A large living room (>= 40 m2) may carry a wardrobe as living_storage; do not flag a wardrobe in a living room of that size as a wrong-type placement.

A wet fixture is typed from the drawn fixture in its own room, not from the size table of a piece in another room; when the plan shows a shower, the wet fixture is a shower even if a size match elsewhere suggests a tub.
An interior bathroom camera must frame the room's full fixture set (WC, basin, storage, bath/shower) from a corner with headroom, never a single fixture in isolation.
A bathroom whose documents draw a tub block (parent-bath set) must be built with a bathtub, not a shower, even when the room is small.
A shoe_cabinet belongs at an entrance hall, not at a top-floor landing; a landing hall takes a console or storage instead.
A balcony/terrace larger than about 12 m2 must be furnished as a seating set (at least two seats plus a table), never a single chair.
A WC flush plate must render as a slim rounded dual-flush plate with a small and a large button, never as a frame holding two flat panes.
An accent wall finish (e.g. vertical slats) is applied to at most one wall of a room, never to all walls of a room or to every room.
An interior camera must frame at least one fixture or piece of value, never a bare wall, corner or switch.
A facade scheme with a stone base and a render body must keep the stone to the base/plinth and apply the render (e.g. white) to the upper walls, never stone from base to eaves.
An interior camera must frame the room's built fixtures; a black/empty view is a camera failure, not a missing room.
A site area drawn in the documents (pool, terrace, parking) must be built with an outline and tracked as a site area, even when its geometry is already present in the model.
The sheets stage must resolve every sheet question before ending; a run that ends 'pending' with open questions has not finished its reading.
A sofa's front is its long side facing the most open room; a front read on its short side (an AI front) is a reading error and must be corrected to the long side.
A drawn piece whose size and wall position match a console table (long, narrow, back on a wall) must be typed console_table, not bench, so its front faces the room and its back rests on the wall.
The big loop must run additional cycles when the first cycle yields no gain, to allow the agent to resolve remaining orientation and placement conflicts.
A sofa drawn with its long side against a wall must have its front facing into the room (away from the wall), not along the long side.
A sofa without a front must have its front set to face the most open floor, towards its partner.
An armchair without a front must have its front set to face away from its wall or towards its partner.
An interior camera must be placed at a free point clear of walls and tall proxies, showing the required elements.
A table_coffee built below the library level must be swapped to a library model that fits the piece's dimensions and room.
A tv_unit built below the library level must be swapped to a library model that fits the piece's dimensions and room.
A tall_cabinet built below the library level must be swapped to a library model that fits the piece's dimensions and room.

When no library model passes the fit rules for a piece, the fitter must not silently keep the parametric mesh as if it were a library pick; it must either relax the height/cap tolerance to accept the nearest library model or flag the piece as unbuildable, never report a library-level build from a parametric fallback.

When a tall piece is placed under a sloped ceiling and its height exceeds the local ceiling clearance, the fitter must either lower the piece to a location with sufficient headroom, swap to a model within the clearance, or flag the placement as infeasible; it must not keep a parametric mesh that violates the ceiling.
A camera of a stair room must be posed from the landing or the hall side so the flight is visible, never from a point inside the stair core.
Views flagged for review are a queue, not a defect; each is resolved by the specific camera or door finding that names it.
Every inside door is built open by default (leaf out of the wall) unless a camera or privacy rule closes it; the build records a leaf state for each door it places.
When a camera looks through an inside door into a room worth showing, the build opens that door (leaf out of the view) and records the state.

A nightstand is placed on the free side of the bed head, not in front of a window; when the bed head is against a window wall the nightstand goes on the opposite side or the window is treated as the head wall.
A toilet is built with its base at floor level (lowest point within -0.005..+0.01 m of the room floor); a model whose base sits above the floor is rejected at fit, not swapped in.
A bathroom washbasin is always built with a mirror above it as part of the vanity set; the bathroom set is incomplete without the mirror.
A tv_unit is placed with its back on a wall; when the only free wall span is blocked by doors or windows, the unit is placed on the next free span or the room is flagged, never left floating.
A coffee table is placed in the seating group with a clear gap to every armchair; when the group is too tight, the armchair is re-posed, not the table pushed into it.
A wardrobe is placed with at least 0.80 m clear in front; when the room cannot give that, the wardrobe is moved to a wall with more clearance or the room is flagged, never left short.
A drawn armchair in a seating group is re-posed (rotated) to face the group and clear its front zone before it is moved; a move beyond the drawn lock is refused, so rotation is the first fix.

rules_proposed.rule: When a room label is read from the plan, the room outline it anchors must be built into the model; a label with no matching room outline is a lost room, not a detail to skip.

When a drawn piece is already typed and is drawn largely inside a larger piece of the same type in the same room, treat it as a duplicate of that piece (one item drawn twice) and drop the smaller one, instead of keeping it as a second piece that cannot be built.

When a drawn piece is already typed and is drawn largely inside a larger piece of a different type in the same room, treat it as a part of that piece (e.g. a seat cushion) and drop it, instead of keeping it as a separate piece that cannot be built.
A stair room whose stair fills the room and whose only camera point is inside the stair is shown by the adjacent hall's camera, not by its own interior camera.
Every drawn piece that is not built must be explained by a warning, a review entry or a symbol record; an untyped piece left unexplained is a loss.
none
The reading stage should read entities on off or frozen layers when the ledger shows they hold geometry the model needs, or explicitly record why they are excluded.
The reading stage should read or explicitly skip entity types like OLE2FRAME and WIPEOUT, recording the reason for the skip.
A camera dropped by the camera stage must carry a reason; a drop with no reason is a loss that must be restored or explained.
A window that is not visible in a view that must show it is a render framing issue; the render stage should adjust the view or flag the window as occluded.
A drawn block that no model element uses must be either mapped to a model element or recorded as a non-structural annotation with a reason.
Anonymous A$C-prefixed blocks under 0.3 m on a side are annotation/dimension fragments, not furniture: the reading stage must not list them as lost furniture.

A drawn block whose name is not a known furniture symbol and whose size matches a standard piece (e.g. ~0.8 x 0.8 m) must be typed by the reading stage from its size and room before it is dropped; untyped blocks of furniture size are a reading loss, not a detail.

A drawn block whose name is not a known furniture symbol and whose size matches a standard piece (e.g. ~1.6 x 2.9 m, a bed or sofa) must be typed by the reading stage from its size and room before it is dropped; untyped blocks of furniture size are a reading loss, not a detail.

A drawn block whose name is not a known furniture symbol and whose size matches a standard piece (e.g. ~0.6 x 0.6 m, a chair or table) must be typed by the reading stage from its size and room before it is dropped; untyped blocks of furniture size are a reading loss, not a detail.
A block recorded as site decor (sd_*) is intentionally not built into the house model; the ledger must not flag it as lost furniture.
A drawn block named for a building element (e.g. 'merdiven' = stair) must be typed as that element by the reading stage; a stair-sized block left untyped is a reading loss.

A drawn block whose name is a placeholder or annotation string (not a furniture/fixture symbol) and whose size does not match any room program is not a lost element; the reading may drop it without building it.
Auto-generated block names (prefix 'A$C') are annotation or leader artifacts, not furniture; the reading may drop them without building them.
A drawn block whose name is not a recognized furniture or fixture symbol and whose footprint does not correspond to a missing required piece in its room is not a lost element.
Entities on layers that are off or frozen in the source DWG are intentionally hidden by the author; the reading correctly skips them and they are not lost elements.
OLE2FRAME and WIPEOUT entities are not furniture or fixtures; the reading correctly does not build them.
Reading diagnostics about wall layer selection, column counts, and stroke pairing are informational warnings, not lost elements.
A symbol that both reading passes classify as not_furniture and keep as an obstacle is a correct reading decision, not a lost element.
A drawn element on a structural layer (e.g. 'A-BA') classified as a column is structure, not furniture; the reading correctly does not build it as a furniture piece.

When one room outline carries the labels of two or more rooms, the reading must split it at the missing wall before room assignment; a label with no matching room outline is a lost-room signal, not a duplicate.
A piece placed by the decor stage must survive the agent stage; if the agent drops it, it must be re-added.
The agent stage must not drop a placed decor piece without recording it; a piece present after the decor stage and absent after the agent stage is a loss to be restored, not silently removed.

A stove that is a member of a kitchen run (module:kitchen_counter:kitchen_run) must be built as part of that run's model, not as a standalone object; the build stage must emit the run's full model (counter, sink, stove) so every planned member has a scene object.

A sink_kitchen that is a member of a kitchen run (module:kitchen_counter:kitchen_run) must be built as part of that run's model, not as a standalone object; the build stage must emit the run's full model (counter, sink, stove) so every planned member has a scene object.

When two drawn pieces of the same type overlap by more than 30% and one is clearly inside the other, the smaller is a duplicate drawing of the same object, not a second piece; the larger is kept and the smaller is dropped as a detail.

When two drawn pieces of the same type overlap by more than 15% and one is clearly inside the other, the smaller is a duplicate drawing of the same object, not a second piece; the larger is kept and the smaller is dropped as a detail.
A small piece drawn 80% or more inside a larger seating piece (armchair, sofa) is its seat cushion or built-in element, not a separate piece; it is dropped as a detail of the larger piece.

A room whose program is a stair core (stair fills the room, no free floor point) is not given an interior camera; it is shown by the adjacent hall's view instead, and the camera stage must skip it rather than report it as a lost view.

A drawn block in a kitchen whose size matches a small appliance (roughly 0.2-0.6 m) that the furniture vocabulary does not type must be recorded with an explicit 'appliance, not modelled' note (or a dedicated appliance type) so it is neither silently dropped nor left unexplained.

A layer whose name is a stair section or elevation view (A-MERDIVEN, A-merdiven görünüş) is a detail view, not plan furniture: the reading classifies it as a detail view and feeds it to the stair reader, and the ledger does not flag it as lost when the stair it documents is built.

A layer whose name is a decorative or sanitary fixture detail view (Deko_Vitrifiye, Piu_Vitrifiye) is a detail view, not plan furniture: the reading classifies it as a detail view and the ledger does not flag it as lost.

rules_proposed.rule: A bedroom's anchor piece (the bed) must be placed inside the room outline; if the solver cannot fit the drawn bed, it must re-solve the sleeping group around the bed's drawn centre rather than dropping the bed.

A balcony's primary furniture group (seating) must be placed inside the room outline; if the solver cannot fit the drawn pieces, it must re-solve the terrace group around the drawn anchor rather than leaving the space empty.
An interior camera of a wet room must frame the room's primary fixtures (toilet, basin, shower/bathtub); a view that omits them is a bare-wall shot and is re-posed to show them.
A bedroom render must show the bed as the room's anchor; a camera that crops the bed out is re-posed to include it.
An interior camera of a wet room must frame the room's primary fixtures; a view that omits them is re-posed to show them.
A bedroom that is furnished with a desk and office chair in addition to a bed is a bedroom with a work corner, not a misread; the presence of the bed_double in the room's piece list is the anchor.
A hall render must show its main piece (shoe cabinet, console, stair); a camera that frames only a bare wall is re-posed to include the anchor.
A balcony or terrace with drawn furniture must have that furniture built and visible; an empty outdoor room is a fit failure, not a camera failure.

A shower drawn with a small gap behind it (its back parallel to the wall) belongs on the wall: the reading snaps its back onto the wall instead of leaving a visible gap.

A shower with less than 0.53 m clear in front is misread: the reading moves it to the nearest valid spot that gives the required front clearance.

rules_proposed.rule: Exterior cameras must be placed at a position and target that frame the house facade or entrance without foreground obstructions (cars, walls, trees) blocking the view.
Interior cameras must be placed at a free point with headroom inside the room, aimed at the room's main fixtures or group, never at a bare wall or outside the room bounds.
A living room's seating and dining sets must be drawn from one style family so the room reads as a designed whole, not a collection of random pieces.
Every bedroom's wall behind the bed must carry a feature finish (panelling or wainscot) to anchor the bed and add depth.
A living room's seating group must be anchored by a large area rug.
A hall must carry a console or a lit wall niche (H1, H4) so it is not a bare passage.
A living room's furniture must form a coherent group; a lone sofa, bench and plant is not a designed room.
A sectional sofa model must be a single welded body; its parts must not stand more than 1 cm apart.
A washbasin's lowest point must sit at floor level (within -0.005..+0.01 m); a model whose base is raised ~0.38 m is a wall-hung unit and must not be placed as a floor-standing basin.
A desk and its office chair must not cut each other; the chair's seat zone must clear the desk by at least the tolerance.
A model-fit check (M33) must not be reported against a piece whose type has no seat or back (e.g. potted_plant, side_table); the check should be skipped for non-seating types.
When a seating model's back or arm is detached from its seat by more than 5 mm (M33), swap to a library model of the same type whose geometry is integral.
A wardrobe model with a large glass pane in its door is not a standard wardrobe; swap to a solid-door wardrobe model of the same type and size.
An interior corridor camera must show the doors or the main circulation path, not a close-up of a wall detail.
A bathroom camera must show the main fixtures (shower, toilet, washbasin) with enough headroom to see the full height of the shower and mirror.
A shower screen must be transparent glass or a textured panel, not a flat opaque slab; swap to a library shower model with a proper glass screen.
A corridor camera must show the doors and circulation path, not a blank corner or featureless wall.
A kitchen render must include small appliances and decor on the worktop to look lived-in, matching the reference.
A wall_cabinet model that renders as a missing or invisible layer must be swapped to a library model that renders correctly.
A kitchen worktop must include small appliances or decor to look functional and lived-in.
A kitchen camera must show the main functional elements (fridge, stove, counter) without cutting them off.
When an armchair's design language clashes with the room's other furniture, swap to a model that matches the room's style.
When a dining table's design language clashes with the room's other furniture, swap to a model that matches the room's style.
A living room with a minimalist style should have a feature wall (fluted or slatted wood panelling) behind the main seating group to anchor it.
A full-height window in a living room must be dressed with layered curtains (a sheer behind a heavier drape) in the render, not left as bare glass.
A coffee table in a living room must be styled (books, a vase, small decor) in the render, never left as a bare surface.
A living room must be lit with layered warm light (downlights plus a warm lamp glow), not a single cold linear pendant and daylight.
A bathroom render must include wall art (a framed piece) so the walls are not bare.
An interior bathroom camera must be pulled back and raised to show the whole room (vanity, shower, toilet), not a low close-up of one fixture.
A window must be dressed with layered curtains (sheer plus drape), not left as bare glass.
A bed must be styled with layered bedding (duvet, throw, a blanket across the foot, euro shams and decorative cushions), not a single duvet and a few pillows.
An interior hall camera must show the hall, its floor and its main group, not be pressed against a wall on a single picture frame.
An office chair in a bedroom must be a calm, warm, light-wood piece that matches the bedroom palette, not a black leather corporate chair.
The wall behind a bed head must be a feature wall (fluted/slatted wood panelling or wainscot), not flat concrete.
A bed must be styled with layered bedding (duvet, euro shams, decorative cushions), not a flat sheet and a single runner.
A bathroom door must be a modern, neutral-toned door that matches the room, not a warm prominent wood door with a large handle.
An interior hall camera must show the room as a whole from a hero angle, not a corner and the side of a single wardrobe.
Armchairs in a living room must share one design era and a palette that harmonises with the sofas, not clashing teal and red pieces.
A coffee table must be a 3D model, never a flat 2D image standing on the floor.
A dining chair and its table must be from the same style family as the rest of the room, not a cheaper white spindle set.
A balcony or terrace program must include at least one potted plant and one soft or lighting element; a bare slab with only seating is not a finished outdoor space.
Upper-floor windows in living and bedroom rooms must carry curtains or blinds in the render; bare glazing reads as unfinished.
An exterior camera must be a clear eye-level (1.5-1.7 m) or a high view above the ridge; it must not be obstructed by a car or interior.
An interior room camera must frame the room's main group (basin, shower, toilet for a bathroom), not a detail crop of a corner.
A model whose back or arm stands more than 5 mm from its seat is a broken model; swap it for a model with a coherent frame.
An interior room camera must frame the room's main group, not a corner with a blank wall.
An interior room camera must frame the room's layout and main pieces, not a wall section and a small cabinet.
A living room with a dining area should have a feature wall (slatted wood or paneling) behind the main seating or dining zone to add depth.
